items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Benny's wife was playing piano, but I don't remember how the band sounded

ctx.x: I was surprised because I had been in plenty of bars in downtown Oakland and nothing like that had happened and perhaps that was the reason unbeknowing to me at the time that I didn't want to go across the street to that bar. That caused me to dislike San Diego and the atmosphere at the Silver Slipper didn't help me to like the town either, because the people in general were not very friendly.

Benny Waters, the tenor sax man that I had worked with in Charlie Johnson Small's Paradise orchestra, was leading a quartet in a cabaret that was strictly for white, but he told me that I could come to hear him, but I would have to sit on the bandstand. I had not seen Benny for years and was surprised to see him so far away from the Apple. I went to see him between one of our sets one night as the place where he was working was one very near the Silver Slipper which should have been called the 'Dirty Slipper!…

We finally finished in San Diego and came to Los Angeles where we stayed in a hotel on First Street and San Pedro which I was told was the Japanese quarters before the Second World War began or before the Japanese bombarded Pearl Harbor. After a few days, the hotel started jumping because some of the musicians from Eddie Heywood, Jr.'s orchestra were staying there and Buster Bailey and myself got together every day with Emmett Berry the trumpeter and Keg Purnell the drummer.
